newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel to cut aid to east in 1998 budget - paper.
newsitem.headline: Waigel to cut aid to east in 1998 budget - paper.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel plans to cut 4.5 billion marks ($2.6 billion) in subsidies to the former communist east of the country to help to fill gaping holes in his 1998 budget, a newspaper reported on Tuesday.

The Leipziger Volkszeitung, in a release ahead of publication on Wednesday, said Manfred Kolbe, a deputy in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) from the eastern state of Saxony, vowed to resist such cuts.
"Such massive cuts would mean the broad end of operative economic support and would risk finally bringing the construction of the east to a standstill," he told the paper.

Kolbe said Waigel planned to cut 1.6 billion marks in aid for economic and agriculture infrastructure, 200 million marks for city building work, 60 million marks in industrial aid and 2.5 billion marks for job creation.
Sources in Kohl's ruling coalition said earlier the 1998 budget still needed more work but the amount that needed to be saved had been narrowed down to below 10 billion marks.

Decisions on the 1998 budget, as well as a supplementary budget for 1997, are not expected until next week. Waigel is set to hold separate meetings with ministers and more coalition talks are planned.
Waigel is struggling to make savings to ensure that Germany hits the strict budget deficit target of 3.0 percent of gross domestic product to qualify for Europe's single currency.

He started with a forecast shortfall for 1998 of over 30 billion marks, arising from a weak tax take and high benefit payments to Germany's four million jobless. Much of that will covered by the sale of shares in Deutsche Telekom AG.
Sources in the three parties making up Kohl's centre-right coalition said negotiations were going well, with talks on the defence, transport and agriculture budgets already advanced.

But the sources reported resistance to spending cuts from Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt, who is responsible for state aid to industry, and Labour Minister Norbert Bluem, who wants to defend his welfare budget.
